articles.title: Ten Uniface forms without painting a single field - generating the XML instead
articles.excerpt: The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 had grown to more than a hundred services for sales: products, prices, quotes, orders, invoices, payments, dunning, deliveries, s…
articles.body: The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 had grown to more than a hundred services for sales: products, prices, quotes, orders, invoices, payments, dunning, deliveries, subscriptions, bank statements. None of it had a user interface yet. The next stage was ten new forms with between 11 and 58 fields each - 310 fields in total - plus one new button in the existing main menu. Painting 310 fields one by one in the form painter is slow, and it is hard to keep a consistent layout. The IDE can export and import repository objects as XML, so the forms were generated as XML and imported instead. This article shows how that worked, what the form picture inside the XML looks like, and the one mistake that crashed the IDE.
articles.author: Franz

articles.title: Step-Up Authentication for Sensitive Actions
articles.excerpt: A few years ago a client's support team got a call from a customer whose payout bank account had been changed overnight. The login itself looked normal: correct password, a known browser, a session th…
articles.body: A few years ago a client's support team got a call from a customer whose payout bank account had been changed overnight. The login itself looked normal: correct password, a known browser, a session that had been open for eleven days on a shared office machine. Someone had simply walked up to an unlocked laptop, opened the billing page and swapped the IBAN. Nothing in our stack asked "are you still you?" before a change that moved real money. The fix was not a stronger password policy. It was step-up authentication on the handful of actions that actually matter. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every snippet against current OWASP Authentication and Session Management cheat sheets, NIST SP 800-63B, the WebAuthn Level 3 spec, Laravel 11 and Node 22.

articles.title: Packing a Freelance Delivery Zip: Strip Secrets, node_modules and Editor Junk with a Small Node Script
articles.excerpt: The last thing I do on a freelance web job, after the site works and the client has said it looks good, is pack the files. That sounds simple. It is not, if you pack the wrong folder. I have almost se…
articles.body: The last thing I do on a freelance web job, after the site works and the client has said it looks good, is pack the files. That sounds simple. It is not, if you pack the wrong folder. I have almost sent a client a zip that still had a .env file in it. I have also sent zips that included node_modules , a .DS_Store , an editor folder and a debug log. None of those help the client. Some of them can cause real trouble. A secret in a delivery zip is still a secret that left your machine. I'm a freelance full-stack developer in Karachi, and I now treat the delivery zip as its own small task, with a script I can run the same way every time.

articles.title: Your Self Assessment Is Due on Friday and You Do Not Know What to Write
articles.excerpt: The annual review form has arrived. Before your manager writes anything, you are asked to assess yourself. What did you achieve this year? Where did you grow? What would you do differently? There are…
articles.body: The annual review form has arrived. Before your manager writes anything, you are asked to assess yourself. What did you achieve this year? Where did you grow? What would you do differently? There are three empty boxes and a deadline on Friday, and you cannot remember what you did in March. Many people treat this form as a chore, write a few modest lines, and hope their manager remembers the rest. It is worth more effort than that. Your manager may be writing reviews for eight or ten people at once, and your self assessment is often the most detailed record they have of your year. What you write can shape what they write. Start by gathering evidence, not by writing. Go through your calendar, your closed tickets, your merged pull requests and the documents you wrote, month by month.

articles.body: Last spring a former teammate of mine applied to 140 roles in six weeks. He got four replies, all automated rejections. Then he sent one short message to someone he had worked with three years earlier, who now led a platform team at a mid-size SaaS company. Nine days later he had an offer. Same resume, same skills, same market. The only difference was that a person inside the company put his name in front of the hiring manager with one sentence of context. In a flooded applicant pool, that sentence is worth more than any keyword. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked the advice against what I have seen work as a hiring manager, a referrer and a candidate.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.title: Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect
articles.excerpt: "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon. Everyone is very confident on this."
articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.
